blocks.text: A 27-year-old has missed work every month since she was 16 because of period pain that no paracetamol touches. She has been told it is 'just painful periods'. Her pain now also happens on intercourse and when she opens her bowels during menses. Chronic cyclical pelvic pain is often an unrecognised disease with a typical pattern, whereas a teenager who collapses with sudden one-sided pain and vomiting may have only hours to save an ovary. This unit separates the two.

blocks.markdown:
**Acute pelvic pain** (new, usually under a week) in a woman of reproductive age has a short list of dangerous causes. The first step is always a **pregnancy test**, because ectopic pregnancy is life-threatening and changes everything else. Then think of: **ovarian torsion**, **pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)**, ruptured or haemorrhagic ovarian cyst, appendicitis, urinary tract infection and renal colic, and degeneration of a fibroid.

**Chronic pelvic pain** is pelvic pain persisting for about 6 months or more. Its causes cross organ systems: **endometriosis**, **adenomyosis**, pelvic adhesions (after surgery or PID), residual or chronic PID, **irritable bowel syndrome**, interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome), pelvic floor myofascial pain, and neuropathic or psychological contributors. A focused history looks for **cyclicity** (links to menses), relation to bowel, bladder and intercourse, and red flags such as postcoital or postmenopausal bleeding.

blocks.title: Endometriosis and fibroids
blocks.text: Endometriosis is the presence of endometrium-like tissue (glands and stroma) outside the uterine cavity, most often on the ovaries, pelvic peritoneum, uterosacral ligaments and pouch of Douglas, provoking a chronic inflammatory response. Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are benign monoclonal tumours of smooth muscle and fibrous tissue, classified as submucosal, intramural or subserosal by their position in the uterine wall.

blocks.markdown:
**Endometriosis.** The leading explanation is **retrograde menstruation** (Sampson's theory): menstrual endometrial fragments pass through the tubes into the pelvis and implant; additional mechanisms such as coelomic metaplasia and immune factors explain why it develops in only some women. The ectopic tissue responds to oestrogen, bleeds cyclically and causes inflammation, scarring and adhesions. An **endometrioma** is an ovarian cyst containing old blood (a 'chocolate cyst') that shows ground-glass echoes on ultrasound.

**Features.** Cyclical or chronic pelvic pain, severe **dysmenorrhoea**, **deep dyspareunia**, **dyschezia** (painful defaecation) and cyclical bladder symptoms, subfertility, and fatigue. Examination may be normal; with deep disease there may be tender nodules in the uterosacral ligaments or posterior fornix, a fixed retroverted uterus, or an adnexal mass. **Diagnosis**: clinical suspicion, transvaginal ultrasound or MRI for endometrioma or deep disease, and laparoscopy with histology as the traditional reference standard. **Management** is individualised: analgesia (NSAIDs, paracetamol), hormonal suppression (combined hormonal contraception, progestogens, LNG-IUS, GnRH analogues with add-back hormone replacement), and surgery (excision or ablation of lesions, cystectomy of endometrioma, rarely hysterectomy with oophorectomy). When fertility is wanted, hormonal suppression does not improve fertility, so options include surgery and assisted reproduction (check NICE NG73). **Hormonal treatment is not automatically contraception**: the combined pill and LNG-IUS are contraceptive, but some progestogens used for endometriosis do not reliably suppress ovulation, and GnRH analogues are not reliable contraception, so a woman on a GnRH analogue needs a separate method (non-hormonal, for example copper IUD or condoms) and advice on add-back therapy (check BNF, NICE NG73 and FSRH guidance).

rows: Cyclical pain, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, subfertility
Fixed uterus or nodules; ultrasound or MRI; laparoscopy
Heavy periods, pressure symptoms, enlarged irregular uterus
LNG-IUS, tranexamic acid, GnRH analogue before surgery, myomectomy, embolisation or hysterectomy
Sudden severe unilateral pain, nausea, vomiting
Adnexal mass; ultrasound may show an enlarged ovary but normal Doppler does not exclude
Lower abdominal pain, discharge, fever, dyspareunia
Cervical motion and adnexal tenderness; NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea

blocks.markdown:
**Fibroids.** Common in women of reproductive age, oestrogen- and progesterone-dependent, and more frequent in Black women. Many are asymptomatic. Symptoms: **heavy menstrual bleeding** (especially submucosal), pelvic pressure, urinary frequency, constipation, pain and, with cavity distortion, subfertility or miscarriage. Fibroids can undergo **red degeneration** in pregnancy (haemorrhagic infarction causing focal pain and low-grade fever, managed with analgesia). Treatment depends on symptoms, size, location and fertility wishes: LNG-IUS (if the cavity is not distorted), tranexamic acid, GnRH analogues to shrink fibroids before surgery, hysteroscopic resection (submucosal), myomectomy (fertility-preserving), uterine artery embolisation, or hysterectomy.

**Ovarian torsion** is twisting of the ovary on its vascular pedicle, usually with an ovarian mass over about 5 cm, causing venous then arterial obstruction and ischaemia. It presents with sudden severe unilateral pain, nausea and vomiting. Ultrasound Doppler flow can be normal even with torsion, so diagnosis is clinical, and **urgent laparoscopy with detorsion** preserves the ovary.

**Pelvic inflammatory disease** is ascending infection of the upper genital tract, commonly with *Chlamydia trachomatis*, *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* and anaerobes. Diagnose clinically (lower abdominal pain plus cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, with discharge or fever) and treat early because delay increases sequelae: **tubal damage, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, chronic pelvic pain**, and tubo-ovarian abscess or Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis. An example outpatient regimen (teaching example; check against current BASHH and local guidance) is intramuscular ceftriaxone plus doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days.

blocks.title: Acute pelvic pain with fever
blocks.prompt: A 23-year-old presents with 3 days of lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia and purulent discharge. Temperature is 38.4 C. She is tender in both iliac fossae with cervical motion tenderness. The urine hCG is negative. What is your working diagnosis and plan?

steps.text: Exclude pregnancy first: the negative hCG makes ectopic pregnancy unlikely, so infection becomes more likely. Fever, discharge and bilateral tenderness with cervical motion tenderness form the clinical picture of PID.
Investigate: take high vaginal and endocervical swabs, and NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, with HIV and syphilis screening offered. Do not wait for results; delay increases tubal damage.

Treat with an empirical combination covering gonorrhoea, chlamydia and anaerobes, advise on partner notification and abstinence until treatment completion, and arrange review at 72 hours. Admit if she is systemically unwell, cannot take oral treatment, or a tubo-ovarian abscess is suspected.

blocks.answer: Pelvic inflammatory disease; start empirical antibiotics immediately after taking swabs, with partner notification and follow-up.

blocks.title: Planning endometriosis treatment around fertility
blocks.prompt: A 31-year-old with dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and an ultrasound-confirmed 4 cm endometrioma wants contraception and is not planning pregnancy for 3 years. Describe a stepwise plan.

steps.text: Control symptoms: offer NSAIDs and paracetamol and discuss hormonal treatment. Since she needs contraception, continuous combined hormonal contraception or the LNG-IUS is suitable, because reducing cyclical bleeding and hormonal stimulation reduces pain; these methods are also contraceptive, but not every endometriosis progestogen is (check FSRH guidance).

Reassess in 3 months. If pain persists, consider specialist referral, GnRH analogue with add-back therapy (which is not reliable contraception, so she still needs a non-hormonal method), or laparoscopic excision of lesions. A 4 cm endometrioma is monitored or removed if symptomatic or growing.

Plan for fertility later: counsel that hormonal treatment does not damage fertility but does not improve it; when she wishes to conceive, stop suppression and refer early if not pregnant within 12 months (or earlier if older or if pelvic disease is severe).

blocks.answer: Stepwise: analgesia plus continuous hormonal suppression (combined hormonal contraception or LNG-IUS also give contraception; GnRH analogues and some progestogens do not), escalation to GnRH analogue or surgery if refractory, and early fertility counselling.

items: Always check a pregnancy test in acute pelvic pain; ectopic pregnancy must not be missed.
Normal ultrasound or Doppler does not exclude endometriosis or torsion.
Endometriosis pain is typically cyclical and associated with deep dyspareunia and dyschezia.
Treat suspected PID early without waiting for test results, and treat partners.
Match fibroid treatment to symptoms, location and fertility wishes.

blocks.title: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis
blocks.text: Do not delay surgery for imaging in a woman with sudden severe unilateral pain, vomiting and an adnexal mass. A normal Doppler study does not exclude torsion, and prompt detorsion can preserve the ovary even after several hours of symptoms.

points: Acute pelvic pain requires an immediate pregnancy test and consideration of ectopic pregnancy, torsion, PID, cyst accident and non-gynaecological causes.

Chronic pelvic pain has gynaecological (endometriosis, adenomyosis, adhesions), gastrointestinal, urological and musculoskeletal causes; a cyclical pattern with deep dyspareunia suggests endometriosis.
Endometriosis is managed with analgesia, hormonal suppression and surgery according to symptoms and fertility wishes; fibroid treatment depends on symptoms, size, location and fertility.
Ovarian torsion needs urgent laparoscopy; PID needs prompt empirical antibiotics, partner management and follow-up to limit infertility and ectopic risk.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old presents with acute lower abdominal pain. Which investigation should be done immediately in every case before further decision-making?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pregnancy, especially ectopic pregnancy, must be excluded first.
distractorRationale.b: CA-125 is a non-specific marker and has no role in initial assessment of acute pain.
distractorRationale.c: Laparoscopy is invasive and reserved for selected cases after assessment.
distractorRationale.d: MRI is not a first-line test in acute pain.

questions.explanation: Ectopic pregnancy is the most dangerous cause of acute pelvic pain in a woman of reproductive age and is identified by a positive hCG. A rapid, cheap pregnancy test also changes imaging and drug choices.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old has had lower abdominal pain for 18 months, with bloating and altered bowel habit; pain is eased by opening her bowels and does not vary with her menstrual cycle. Pelvic examination and ultrasound are normal. Which cause is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: chronic pelvic pain with bloating, altered bowel habit and relief on defaecation with a normal gynaecological assessment suggests IBS.
distractorRationale.b: Torsion is acute and severe, not 18 months of pain.
distractorRationale.c: Acute PID presents with fever and discharge over days.
distractorRationale.d: Red degeneration occurs usually in pregnancy and is acute.

questions.explanation: Chronic pelvic pain commonly has a non-gynaecological source. Features linking pain to bowel function, lack of cyclicity and a normal examination and scan favour irritable bowel syndrome over endometriosis.

questions.stem: Which finding is most consistent with deep endometriosis on pelvic examination?

options.text: A fixed retroverted uterus with tender nodules in the uterosacral ligaments
A smoothly enlarged, mobile, non-tender uterus of 10 weeks' size
A friable cervix that bleeds on contact
A bluish bulging membrane at the introitus

questions.correctOptionText: A fixed retroverted uterus with tender nodules in the uterosacral ligaments

distractorRationale.a: Correct: adhesions and deep nodules cause fixation and tender uterosacral nodularity.
distractorRationale.b: A smooth enlarged uterus suggests pregnancy or adenomyosis, not nodular fixed disease.
distractorRationale.c: A friable cervix suggests cervical pathology.
distractorRationale.d: A bluish bulging membrane indicates an imperforate hymen.

questions.explanation: Cyclical bleeding and inflammation of ectopic endometrium cause fibrosis and adhesions, which tether the uterus and create tender nodules in the uterosacral ligaments and posterior fornix. The examination may be normal in mild disease, so absence of signs does not exclude endometriosis.

questions.stem: A woman at 14 weeks of pregnancy with a known 8 cm fibroid has 2 days of severe focal uterine pain and a temperature of 37.9 C. Fetal heartbeat is present, and the uterus is tender over the fibroid. Which is the most likely diagnosis and best initial management?

options.text: Red degeneration; analgesia and supportive care
Torsion of the ovary; immediate laparotomy

questions.correctOptionText: Red degeneration; analgesia and supportive care

distractorRationale.a: Correct: red degeneration of a large fibroid in pregnancy causes focal pain and low-grade fever and is managed conservatively.
distractorRationale.b: Torsion causes sudden pain with vomiting and an adnexal mass, not tenderness over a known fibroid.
distractorRationale.c: GnRH analogues are contraindicated in pregnancy and endometriosis does not explain this picture.
distractorRationale.d: PID is rare in an established pregnancy and not suggested by focal fibroid tenderness.

questions.explanation: Rapid growth in pregnancy can outstrip a fibroid's blood supply, causing haemorrhagic infarction. Pain and low-grade fever settle with analgesia and rest, and the pregnancy usually continues.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old has sudden severe right-sided pelvic pain with vomiting. Ultrasound shows a 7 cm ovarian cyst, with ovarian Doppler flow present. Pregnancy test is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent laparoscopy with detorsion because normal Doppler does not exclude torsion
Discharge with analgesia since Doppler flow is present
Start oral antibiotics for pelvic inflammatory disease

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent laparoscopy with detorsion because normal Doppler does not exclude torsion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the clinical picture and mass suggest torsion; preserved Doppler flow does not exclude it.
distractorRationale.b: Discharge risks ovarian loss from ischaemia.
distractorRationale.c: PID presents with fever and discharge, not sudden severe unilateral pain with a large cyst.
distractorRationale.d: Delay risks infarction of the ovary.

questions.explanation: Partial or intermittent torsion can preserve Doppler flow because the ovary has dual blood supply and arterial inflow persists until late. Surgical exploration is guided by clinical suspicion, and detorsion conserves the ovary.

questions.stem: True or false: when pelvic inflammatory disease is suspected clinically, antibiotic treatment should be started without waiting for the chlamydia and gonorrhoea results.
questions.explanation: Delayed treatment of PID increases the risk of tubal damage, ectopic pregnancy and infertility, and test results can take days. Swabs are taken first, then empirical treatment starts and is adjusted if needed.

questions.stem: Ultrasound measures a uterine fibroid at 7.0 cm x 5.0 cm x 4.0 cm. Using the ellipsoid formula V = 0.5236 x a x b x c, calculate the fibroid volume in cm^3.
questions.explanation: V = 0.5236 x 7.0 x 5.0 x 4.0 = 0.5236 x 140 = 73.3 cm^3. Volume rather than a single diameter is used to follow growth or the response to treatment such as a GnRH analogue, because small changes in diameter give large changes in volume.

questions.stem: Describe the diagnosis, treatment and complications of pelvic inflammatory disease, and explain the importance of partner management.
markingGuide: Ascending infection from the cervix, commonly Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae and anaerobes
Clinical diagnosis: lower abdominal pain with cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, plus discharge or fever; exclude pregnancy
Investigations: NAAT swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, pregnancy test, consider ultrasound for abscess
Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics started promptly (for example ceftriaxone, doxycycline, metronidazole; check against BASHH/local guidance)
Complications: tubal damage, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, chronic pelvic pain, tubo-ovarian abscess, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome
Partner notification and treatment to prevent reinfection and onward spread; abstain from intercourse until treatment complete
Follow up at about 72 hours, admit if severe
questions.explanation: PID is diagnosed clinically because tests are slow and imperfect, and early treatment reduces tubal damage. Treating partners is essential because untreated partners reinfect women and spread infection.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old has been diagnosed with endometriosis and is trying to conceive. Describe how her treatment differs from that of a woman who needs contraception, and explain the reasoning.
markingGuide: Hormonal suppression (combined pill, progestogens, GnRH analogues) reduces pain by suppressing ovarian hormone cycles and cannot be used while trying to conceive; note that hormonal treatment is not automatically contraception: the combined pill and LNG-IUS are contraceptive, but GnRH analogues are not reliable contraception and some progestogens do not reliably suppress ovulation
Hormonal suppression does not improve fertility
Analgesia with NSAIDs and paracetamol can be used while trying to conceive (NSAIDs may need review)
Surgical excision or ablation of lesions or endometrioma removal may improve pain and the chance of natural conception in selected cases, with caution about ovarian reserve
Referral for assisted reproduction (IUI or IVF) if conception fails or disease is severe
questions.explanation: Most medical therapy treats pain by suppressing ovarian hormone cycles (and often ovulation), so it is incompatible with conception and does not improve fertility. Planning therefore relies on analgesia, selective surgery and early referral for assisted conception.

questions.stem: Compare the common causes of acute and chronic pelvic pain in women of reproductive age. For acute pain, identify the three diagnoses that need urgent recognition and the feature that distinguishes each.
markingGuide: Acute causes: ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, PID, cyst rupture or haemorrhage, appendicitis, urinary tract disease
Chronic causes (6 months or more): endometriosis, adenomyosis, adhesions, irritable bowel syndrome, bladder pain syndrome, musculoskeletal and neuropathic pain
Ectopic pregnancy: positive pregnancy test, amenorrhoea, vaginal bleeding, possible shock
Torsion: sudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting and an adnexal mass
PID: fever, discharge and bilateral tenderness with cervical motion tenderness
Pregnancy test first; ultrasound; use cyclicity and relationship to bowel and bladder to categorise chronic pain
questions.explanation: Acute pelvic pain demands rapid identification of ectopic pregnancy, torsion and PID, each with a distinguishing feature and a different treatment. Chronic pain needs a broader, multi-system assessment where cyclicity and pain triggers point to the gynaecological, bowel or bladder source.
